Marcelo Mello , Paula Serafim , Maira Moraes , Agnes Miranda , Yusaku Soussumi and Andrea Mello

Andrea Mello

Sao Paulo, Brazil

São Paulo, Brazil

Rua Botucatu, 431 Sao Paulo-SP Brazil ZIP 04023-061 (email: mf-mello@uol.com.br).

Andrea Mello  

cortisol, maternal deprivation, risk factor, neonatal stress

Early life experiences may have enduring effects on human biological development. Premature infants aged 6 to 12 months cared for in incubators (control group, C) shortly after delivery were compared with premature newborns cared for using the kangaroo method (experimental group, E), characterized by consistent skin-to-skin contact. We found that groups C (n = 15) and E (n = 27) were comparable at birth. Logistic regression analysis showed that Group C infants had higher salivary cortisol concentrations and were shorter as compared with Group E infants. These findings are consistent with experimental findings showing that differences on early maternal presence lead to enduring biological consequences.

The Neural Basis of the Dynamic Unconscious: Response to Commentaries

Heather Berlin

Heather Berlin

Heather Berlin  

unconscious, psychodynamic, repression, suppression, dissociation, neural

Building a Better “Neuropsychoanalytic” Bridge

First and foremost, I would like to thank the commentators for their very insightful responses. Most of them suggested helpful enhancements and refinements of my arguments, which are very much appreciated. I will make some remarks on a few general themes that ran across many of the replies as well as address some specific points.

Morris Eagle highlighted the differences between the dynamic unconscious, which he describes as involving “unconscious emotional and motivational factors that can mold the unconscious mind,” and the descriptive (Freud) or cognitive unconscious. He claims that many of the studies I cite support the concept of ubiquitous unconscious processing, but do not test directly the “dynamic unconscious.” I appreciate this distinction, and while I do cite studies that show that unconscious affective and motivational factors can mold and shape cognition and behavior, it is harder to determine empirically how unconscious affective and motivational factors can mold and shape the unconscious mind, which is central to processes like repression. However, if everything is taking place outside of awareness—that is, both the input and output, or the independent and dependent variables—how can we measure these phenomena in the lab? Researchers can begin to resolve this conundrum by devising inventive paradigms to accurately test the neural basis of unconscious defense mechanisms experimentally. But they must also work together with analysts who can help to better define the concepts scientists are trying to quantify.

For example, Eagle points out that repression may not be a unitary process and may, in fact, be referring to a wide range of phenomena, each of which may involve different psychological processes and therefore different corresponding neural processes. Accordingly, there are mixed results and inconsistent findings with regard to the relationship between repressive style and psychological and physical stress. Some studies show that people with a repressive style have fewer psychological, somatic, and health problems than those with a nonrepressive style, while other studies show the opposite results. This may be related to differences in methodology—for example, how repressive style is measured—or it may be that repression is initially beneficial, but the negative effects may emerge over the long term.

Neuropsychoanalytic Clinical Study Center of NPAP (The National Association for Psychoanalysis), New York

Sally Lord

Sally Lord

slord1@nyc.rr.com

Sally Lord  

Our group is now in its eighth year studying the psychoanalytic treatment of brain-injured patients. Coordinated by Edith Laufer and supervised by Mark Solms with Anna Chapman, consulting psychiatrist, and Walter Nieves, neurologist, we primarily treat patients with focal brain lesions. At times we have also included other conditions such as epilepsy.

Recently some of our therapists gave progress reports on their cases. All agreed that this work presented challenges that went beyond those presented by more typical analytic patients. The following are brief examples:

A 64-year-old male underwent a craniotomy resection after suffering a seizure due to a subfrontal olfactory groove meningioma. Diffuse swelling occurred, and the patient was placed in a barbiturate coma to monitor intercranial pressure. Following this the patient recovered, but not sufficiently to return to his former work as a high-functioning professional. Moreover, he found himself without the vital sense of agency that had characterized his entire previous life. In therapy he made visible gains, showing increased energy and confidence and becoming far less dependent on his caretaker wife. Although apparently pleased with the accomplishments of his treatment, he expressed no interest in exploring any of the premorbid psychological issues that emerged, and these were left unexamined.

A 78-year-old woman suffered a large middle artery stroke that left her with global aphasia. Intensive rehabilitation, including an aphasia group, enabled her to regain limited speech. In therapy the patient displayed disabling anxiety with emotional flooding and frequently canceled sessions. A distrust of authority stemming from her early upbringing in a totalitarian Eastern European state was exacerbated by intense feelings of helplessness engendered by the stroke. The confluence of these elements seemed not only to prevent the patient from establishing a real alliance with the therapist, but also to interfere with her understanding of the treatment process itself, and she left treatment prematurely.

Richard Kessler

Richard Kessler

NY, U.S.A.

Richard Kessler  

hallucinatory wish-fulfilment, hallucination, primary process, sensory feedback, theta rhythm

Siri Hustvedt's work illustrates how psychoanalysis offers unique and crucially important insights in the study of fundamental issues in human psychology such as those of memory, perception, subjectivity, and creativity. Her findings dovetail with Freud's concepts of hallucinatory wish-fulfilment and primary process (as further elaborated by psychoanalysts Pinchas Noy and Barry Opatow). The findings also find resonance in a variety of neuroscientific fields of research, especially in studies of theta rhythm and its role in dreaming, memory, and early mental development, the relationship between hallucination and perception, and the brain research of Rodolfo Llinas.

Psychoanalysis and Neuroscience Chapter of the Argentine Psychoanalytical Association

Finding links between bipolar disorder and personality disorders

Diego Cohen , Lorena Santos , Martín Ruiz , Ricardo Corral , Carolina Vairo and Cíntia Pereira

Cíntia Pereira

diegocohen@fibertel.com.ar

loregsantos@gmail.com

martin.ruiz@hospitalitaliano.org.ar

rcorral@intramed.net.ar

carovairo@hotmail.com

cintiagpereira@hotmail.com

Cíntia Pereira  

The members of our chapter have decided in the last few years to move toward clinical research. After analyzing some reference papers in psychoanalytic research (Emde & Fonagy, 1997; Williams, 1999), we decided to probe some long-standing clinical and psychopathological assertions or those in which the most recent data are inconclusive. We therefore initiated a study to assess the presence or absence of personality disorder during periods of remission in patients with different clinical forms of bipolar disorder (BPD). We have been particularly interested in the theories of Abraham and Kernberg regarding personality organization.

In two Buenos Aires hospitals, we examined a pool of patients with SCID-I and II interviews to determine Axis I and II diagnoses, respectively. Among the patients with bipolar I and bipolar II, some of these patients were determined to have no personality disorders, while other patients did merit an additional diagnosis of personality disorder, including dependent, borderline, obsessive-compulsive, histrionic, and narcissistic personality disorders. Our findings will be submitted for publication in the near future. We believe our findings demonstrate a high degree of association between bipolar disorder and personality disorder. We did not find evidence to support Abraham's hypothesis (1955/1994) about a high degree of association between cyclic disorder and obsessive organization, although Abraham was referring to melancholy (now severe forms of unipolar depression) and our number of cases is low when compared to that form of disorder. We will argue that our findings did partially confirm Kernberg's (1984) hypothesis about the association between bipolar disorder and borderline personality. Patients without personality disorder, it is worth clarifying, still did not necessarily qualify as “normal,” but pathology was not detected by the instrument employed for the assessment.

In a time when there is a great degree of neurobiological dominance in psychopathological explanations, we believe that this study will support a psychoanalytic hypothesis about the close link between character structure and the most important syndromatic states. Our findings are resonant with the results of Blatt (2008), who points out two primary configurations of personality organization: (1) introjective and (2) anaclitic. The high degree of association between bipolar disorder and dependent disorder leads to the second type of psychopathology corresponding to “anaclitic depression.

Reports from the Twelfth International Neuropsychoanalysis Congress

Aidan Lunt

Aidan Lunt

Leicester, U.K.

Aidan Lunt  

The 2011 International Neuropsychoanalysis Congress, with its theme of exploring the embodiment of the self, was held in Berlin. The city has a divided past, of which there are constant reminders as you walk around, and a present that following reunification is slowly healing together these once separate parts. The congress venue was a splendidly restored Berlin Water Services pumping station, built at the turn of the last century and now converted into an arts and conference centre.

The setting of this once-divided city seemed appropriate, as the conference attempted to address the integration of the mind-body split, with us from Descartes' era and so eloquently described by one of the key speakers in his book, Descartes' Error: “It suggests that thinking, and awareness of thinking, are the real substrates of being. And since we know that Descartes imagined thinking as an activity quite separate from the body, it does celebrate the separation of mind, the ‘thinking thing’ (res cogitans), from the nonthinking body, that which has extension and mechanical parts (res extensa)”(Damasio, 1996, p. 248).

This attempted integration was approached through an exploration of the way that the body is represented in the brain and the mind—how self-other distinctions are made, allowing us to maintain a sense of self that is distinct from our surroundings (human and nonhuman), while allowing us to understand others' perspectives and differentiate between them and our own.

In the International Neuropsychoanalysis Congresses over the years, I have come to understand the value of the Educational Day. This provides the important background information from both neuroscience and psychoanalysis relevant to the topic under investigation, which orientates participants and allows them to take in more from the congress itself. This year was no exception, with four fascinating presentations setting the scene.

Oliver Turnbull gave a very helpful overview of the representation of the body in the brain, from cortex to brainstem. Beginning with the cortex and motor and sensory homunculi, he demonstrated with the help of the London Underground map the importance of the nature and form of the mapping to the understanding of the underlying structures, by illustrating what was missing and duplicated. He introduced the further homunculi in the thalamus and cerebellum and through these the importance of the interplay between these multiple maps, the links between perception and action in association areas, and the importance of overlapping mapping to clinical conditions including autopagnosia, hemispatial neglect, and phantom limbs.

Slawomir Murawiec  

The group reactivated our monthly meetings on neuropsychoanalysis in November 2010. The subject of the first meeting was the neurobiology of romantic love, attachment, pair bonding, mate choice, and rejection (Dr. Cezary Zechowski). The second was dedicated to Mark Solms's lecture, “What Is Neuropsychoanalysis?” based on minutes from the Paris NPSA Congress. Records of both of them are available on the Internet. Dr. Zechowski's lecture had over 250 visitors in the first month (http://www.ustream.tv/recorded/10674909).

A session entitled “Neuropsychoanalysis” was held at the 43rd Congress of Polish Psychiatrists in Poznan, 23-26 June 2010. The first chapter about neuropsychoanalysis in Polish was published in a textbook for psychology students (Murawiec, 2010).

The Neuropsychoanalysis Group of Mexico City started activity just after the Berlin Congress, where the three current members presented developments in their research projects. The group intends to focus on integrating psychoanalytic methods into empirical studies, hoping to attract colleagues as more work is organized and published.

In terms of our active members, Maria Isabel Rodriguez Luna is a psychologist with a Master of Arts in Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy who has been studying clinical applications of neuropsychoanalysis. At the Tenth Neuropsychoanalysis Congress, she presented a model that includes neurofeedback entitled “The Psychotherapy of Play and Neurofeedback—the Relational Model: The Parent-Child Relationship.” Developing this interdisciplinary model, which integrates psychiatric and psychoanalytic approaches, she presented preliminary findings in a poster at the recent Neuropsychoanalysis Congress in Berlin, exploring the mind-body relation.

Jesùs Baca Plasencia is also a Mexican psychologist; he has trained as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist, and has worked in the field for six years. Currently finishing his doctoral dissertation at Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Spain, he is working with a multidisciplinary focus that integrates philosophical, psychoanalytic, and neurobiological approaches to the problem of the mind-body relation. His work focuses on the genesis of the ego, evaluating the Freudian theory that asserts an evolutionarily derived set of mechanisms whereby the ego arises from the body, including a role for psychic energy in this new creation. This project attempts to take into account the most recent neurobiological findings about the formation of subjective structure that provide the human organism with a sense of self-integration and individuality. At the Berlin Congress, he presented a poster with Prof. Rosario Garcia Cordovilla from the Biological Sciences faculty of Universidad Complutense de Madrid about his ongoing research.

The Scientific Study of Unconscious Processes: The Time is Ripe for (Re)Convergence of Neuroscientific and Psychoanalytic Conceptions

Eric Fertuck

Eric Fertuck

New York, U.S.A.

Eric Fertuck  

unconscious, implicit, psychoanalysis, cognitive neuroscience, neuropsychoanalysis

Psychoanalytic and scientific conceptions of unconscious processes are reconverging. This commentary on Heather Berlin's Target Article, “The Neural Basis of the Dynamic Unconscious,” discusses the current status of the study of the neural substrates of cognitive, affective, and motivational dimensions of unconscious processes. The current research is contextualized with some thoughts on the historical tensions between psychoanalytic and academic models of the mind. Recommendations for advancing both psychoanalytic and neuroscientific investigations of unconscious processes are proposed, with a focus on psychopathology and psychoanalytic treatments and processes in different types of pathological personality structures.

Editors' Introduction

Oliver Turnbull and David Olds

David Olds

David Olds  

This issue is dominated by ORIGINAL ARTICLES, opening with the general theme of “What Is Neuropsychoanalysis?” (Solms & Turnbull), which outlines the scope of our discipline and its philosophical and experimental basis and defines the interesting question of what neuropsychoanalysis is not. We also publish a number of articles on more specific themes: models of change in borderline personality disorder (Viviani et al.), language and the unconscious (Bazan), and the effects of maternal stress (Mello et al).

We also include an article by the acclaimed author Siri Hustvedt, who has a growing interest in neuropsychoanalysis. Indeed, her books increasingly show themes and characters with a neuropsychoanalytic flavor. It is therefore of great interest to see her thoughts on writing, memory, mind, and brain—which we publish with commentaries by Vittorio Gallese and Richard Kessler.

In this issue we have, as ever, our DIGEST, BULLETIN, and BOOK REVIEWS sections. The latter contains a review by Jaak Panksepp of Antonio Damasio's latest book, Self Comes to Mind: Constructing the Conscious Brain, with a response by Damasio himself. Historically minded readers will recall a similar review and response by Panksepp and Damasio in relation to Damasio's previous book—Looking for Spinoza—in our 2003: 2 issue.

A further addition to this issue of the Journal is the publication of Congress Research Presentations from Seattle (2010) and Berlin (2011). The growth in our research presentation numbers has been enormous (see the graph on p. 232) and is a testament to the remarkable growth of the research side of our inter-discipline—an important and most welcome development. To view the Berlin Congress in the round, readers will also be interested in a pair of Congress Reports, which review the content of the Berlin Congress and offer a flavor of the atmosphere surrounding the event.

We are confident that, amid the diversity of offerings in this issue, our readers will find many articles of interest.

Enid Young

Enid Young

drenidyoung@yahoo.com

Enid Young  

The California Neuropsychoanalysis Research Group (CNRG), a nonprofit organization located in Berkeley, California, has grown out of the great need for long-term treatment for those who suffer with neurological issues, particularly traumatic brain injury (TBI). We are committed to offering long-term individual and group work for TBI patients and their families. The CNRG has spent the past three years focused on the relevance of working on self-identity issues through psychoanalytic treatment in the rehabilitation of TBI. We are also interested in researching and treating the coincidence of TBI and PTSD, as well as introducing a psychoanalytic approach to the treatment of chronic pain. The membership of the group consists of Thomasine McFarlin, M.S.W., L.C.S.W.; Joy Ragon, M.A., J.D., R.N.; Nancy Ulmer, M.S.W., L.C.S.W., and Enid Young, Ph.D.

Our objectives are to: promote a better understanding of psychoanalysis and encourage effective and innovative dissemination of psychoanalytic ideas and services to the public; provide practitioners with an essential vocabulary and a basic overview of the clinical and humanistic perspective informed by psychoanalysis; demonstrate how psychoanalytic concepts can be applied to treating TBI patients in preparation for cognitive behavioral and other forms of treatment; train practitioners in the theory and practice of psychoanalysis as applied to the repercussions of TBI, such as the difficulties associated with self-identity and theory-of-mind capacities; promote research connected to the coincidence of TBI and PTSD; explore further research into the integration of the psychodynamic approach in the treatment and clinical management of TBI; improve the accessibility of the psychodynamic approach to treatment of TBI at all levels of rehabilitation; and connect psychoanalytic programs with the Veterans Administration and community programs in order to provide accessible and long-term care to TBI patients and their families.

On 13-14 November 2010, the Psychoanalytic Institute of Northern California, with the participation of the CNRG, presented a conference entitled “Master Clinicians in Neuropsychoanalysis: An Interdisciplinary Approach to Traumatic Brain Injury.” The conference sponsored renowned TBI specialists Dr. Anthony Chen, Dr. Harold Kudler, Dr. Ronald Ruff, and Dr. Oliver Turnbull. On 12 November, Dr. Maggie Zellner presented “Brain Basics of the Psychodynamically Minded: An Introduction to the Brain Systems Every Therapist Should Know.” The aim of the conference was to explore new ideas arising out of the dialogue between neuroscience and psychoanalysis in order to drive forward the field of TBI research and recovery and to develop a shared language that furthers collaboration with TBI rehab practitioners. The conference was resoundingly successful, and we hope to publish several of the papers from the primary speakers in Neuropsychoanalysis.

Larry Kunstadt  

The Body Image Study Group, which operates under the auspices of the Pfeffer Center for Neuropsychoanalysis, met throughout 2010-11 to discuss what biologists call development and psychoanalysts call the genetic point of view.

We went through the history of the nature-nurture problem as debated over most of the twentieth century by European ethologists and American animal behaviorists. The theoretical concepts, which were developed from research on animal behavior, were extrapolated to psychoanalytic theory. We went beyond the original delineation of causal factors arising from internal and external sources (“nature-nurture”) to trying to understand the role of hierarchically organized causal factors including body image. We tried to theorize the application of theories of development of animal behavior to the development of mental life in humans.

The new year began with the profoundly devastating loss of one of our members, Eleanor Galenson, who died at home at the age of 94. Eleanor was one of the most extraordinary people one could ever hope to meet. She was full of life until the end, seeing patients, hosting salons and soirées, attending concerts, meeting with friends, and challenging us all with her vast erudition and intelligence. She was an enthusiastic thinker and questioner. She was at the center of the action for the last half of the century and knew almost all the great people whose ideas comprise the contemporary field of psychoanalysis. We will miss her without end.

In the fall we will begin a year's study of the mind-body problem, where the mind is the psychoanalytic mind and the body is contemporary neurobiology. Our group is tilting a bit toward the geriatric side, and we would encourage one or two young analysts to join us. We meet monthly in New York City.

The Núcleo Tavola Center was founded in 2000 to bring together professionals from various fields in the humanities and psychological sciences, with the aim of promoting interdisciplinary dialog through events, courses, and study groups that take psychoanalysis as the central domain of knowledge. Psychoanalysis has expanded into a multidisciplinary field encompassing biology, psychology, arts, and medicine, requiring that professionals have proper and specific training and, at the same time, remain pluralistic. We do not believe that psychoanalysis is an exclusive practice of doctors and psychologists; on the contrary, we aim to expand the penetration of psychoanalysis in society, constituting an area of permanent development of new forms of psychoanalysis in theory and practice. As Núcleo Tavola has grown considerably in the past ten years, it has been necessary to create departments so that groups of experts could more actively participate in the production and dissemination of knowledge.

The Núcleo Tavola Department of Neuroscience (www.nucleotavola.com.br/neuro) was created in early 2011 with the objective of promoting the interaction between neuroscience and other human sciences and of promoting science to the general population. Specifically, the department organizes courses, study groups, lectures, and other activities on the neurosciences and their interfaces with other areas (including education, psychoanalysis, psychotherapy, and the arts).

Luis Henrique Novaes Milan (psychoanalyst, psychologist, and founder of the Núcleo Tavola) invited Luis Fernando Scozzafave de Souza-Pinto (a psychoanalyst and recently graduated neuroscientist) to set up the group. Souza-Pinto invited fellow neuroscientists to weekly meetings around the theoretical study of “Neuropsychoanalysis” and to organize a regional meeting called “Conferences in Neuroscience and Psychoanalysis,” which will be held on 28 and 29 October 2011. “If the clinical hypothesis is not completely confirmed, the clinician must be willing to reassess the situation and change the treatment. The relentless self-examination that is necessary to achieve this goal is difficult to maintain in an era in which we are increasingly taught to trust only the data obtained by others.” This quote from Dubovsky (2007) refers to industrial influence on psychopharmacological treatment practices. “If the clinical problem itself is poorly defined and obfuscated by marketing strategies, the focus of neurobiological research is set for random effort and misunderstanding” (Fava, 2009).

In an increasingly “evidence-based” environment, what is the clinician to do with the neuroscience data that is increasingly derived using multiple assumptions, frequently questionable, by “experts” in neuroimaging, statistics, and other fields that may be far removed from the clinical encounter? The psychoanalytic component of neuropsychoanalysis potentially provides a counterbalance to possible harm from zealous overapplication.

In a series of lectures to a diverse audience addressing concerns about harmful misapplication of neuroscience, Dr. Jim Deutsch reviewed among other topics those of empathy and the limbic overwhelming of frontal mechanisms in “fight-flight-freeze” situations. A question arose concerning how humans could possibly have “evolved” the capacity to be concerned for the welfare and suffering of those who live on the other side of the globe, even overriding immediate concerns for their own well-being, in these perilous times. A neuroimaging study offers a basis consistent with a developmental progression from representations of manipulable objects to love objects (Zaki, Weber, Bolger, & Ochsner, 2009).

Edward Hug

Edward Hug

Greenfield, MA, U.S.A.

Edward Hug   Psychodramatist in private practice

From 23 to 26 June 2011, Berlin was the venue of the Twelfth International Neuropsychoanalysis Congress, attended by approximately 430 participants from many countries, with the theme of “Minding the Body.” The meetings took place at “radialsystem V,” which opened in 1996 as a new space for the arts on the River Spree in the former East Berlin and functions as a cultural centre “where new ideas ‘radiate’ out in all directions”—an appropriate venue indeed!

Very much appreciated was the current incarnation of the evolving conference structure, with a leading Educational Day, Research Workshops woven into the Congress schedule, and Poster Sessions easily available during intermissions.

The feeling continued at this Twelfth Congress of pushing forward an innovative intellectual frontier by means of an encounter between two rich communities, one—psychoanalysis—a well-established clinical profession and the other—neuroscience—a largely academic profession currently in explosive development. The idea that innovation stems from collaboration and knowledge-sharing across professional or organizational boundaries dates from the 1950s (e.g., Conway, 1995) and is certainly evident at our Congresses.

I cannot do justice in this brief piece to the enormous variety and depth of the presentations, much less to the extremely fertile associations among disciplines, presented and discussed inside and outside the Research Workshops. Here are just a few notes from the Educational Day and the main Congress, neglecting alas the many varied and interesting workshops:

Oliver Turnbull, Manos Tsakiris, Maggie Zellner, and Lisa Ouss conducted the Educational Day, which is a most useful introduction and background-setter for the main Congress. Turnbull reviewed the neuroscience by which the body is represented in the brain. Tsakiris discussed agency and ownership of the body (the right-hemisphere frontal/parietal mediation of own-body perception, illusion mediated by right posterior insula, etc.). Zellner spoke on the brain correlates of the self-other distinction (especially the role of the mirror neuron system and the participation of the temporoparietal junction). Finally, Lisa Ouss discussed disorders falling under the umbrella of hysteria or “conversion disorders,” in which emotional and other psychological dynamics are transferred to or converted into abnormalities in the perception or function of the body, or in dissociative states of consciousness.

The study of emotion regulation has received a lot of interest over the past two decades and, with it, an increasingly sophisticated understanding of the neurobiological processes involved. The primary focus of this literature has been on explicit (i.e., deliberate) emotion regulation, and only recently has there been greater investigation of implicit (i.e., nonconscious) emotion regulation. It is the latter type that is therefore most relevant to an understanding of the neurobiology of the dynamic unconscious, as presented in psychoanalytic theories. In this commentary I summarize the state of knowledge regarding implicit emotion regulation, primarily focusing on experimental paradigms for which neural data have been reported. It is hoped that this perspective will augment Heather Berlin's article, covering other aspects of nonconscious processing relevant to the psychoanalytic concept of the dynamic unconscious.

Models of Change in the Psychotherapy of Borderline Personality Disorders

Roberto Viviani , Horst Kächele and Anna Buchheim

Anna Buchheim

Leimgrubenweg 12, 89075 Ulm, Germany (email: roberto.viviani@uni-ulm.de).

Ulm, Germany

Innsbruck, Austria

Anna Buchheim  

attention, borderline personality disorder, learning, mentalization, proactive interference, semantic memory

Patients suffering from borderline personality disorders are often difficult to treat, and require specific psychotherapeutic techniques. In current neurobiological models of borderline personality disorder, temperamental factors such as increased emotional reactivity and diminished attentional control figure prominently and account for the psychopathology of this disorder. Here, we follow a different approach and ask the question of how a model of this disorder may account for the modifications of psychotherapy technique that have proven effective in this class of patients. The psychotherapy of this disorder emphasizes work on enriching the semantic repertoire of patients in interpreting their own emotion and other people's motivation for their actions. Based on current psychometric research on distinct factors contributing to individual effectiveness in attentional control (working memory capacity), we propose that the organization of semantic memory may constitute an important and neglected aspect of a neurobiological model of this disorder. Impulsivity and emotional dysregulation resemble the long-term developmental effects of habitual strategies to determine response, which cognitive studies have characterized in terms of the interplay of attentional control capacity, cognitive and emotional load, and semantic organization. Rather than attributing an exclusive causal role to either increased emotional reactivity or diminished attentional control, we propose an account of this disorder as emerging from a self-reinforcing developmental history in which both these factors are intertwined. After mapping these notions onto specific psychotherapeutic interventions, we propose a model through which specific technical strategies result, in the long term, in structural change.

International Neuropsychoanalysis Society: Congress Research Presentations, Seattle 2010 and Berlin 2011

Oliver Turnbull and Maggie Zellner

Maggie Zellner

Maggie Zellner  

Research in neuropsychoanalysis has undergone something of a sea-change in the last decade, and the work listed here from recent International Neuropsychoanalysis Congresses demonstrates the remarkable growth in our field.

As is clear from Figure 1, the number of research presentations has increased dramatically over the years since our first meeting, held in 2002 in Stockholm. In part, this is due to some procedural innovations. For example, in 2004 (Rome), it became possible to present posters for the first time, which substantially increased participation. In 2007 (Vienna), we were so struck by demand that it was necessary to introduce parallel sessions for the Oral presentations, again offering increased opportunities for participation. In 2010 (Seattle), we were able to include Oral presentations (previously hosted in a separate Open Research Day) as part of the main Congress.

Through each of these innovations we have attempted to increase the number of participants who are actively engaged in the Congresses. Indeed, we are delighted to report that roughly a quarter of all attendees are now presenters of one sort or another. This is not primarily due to changes in organizational structure, but is an impressive result of the growth of interest in research in our field—a trend that seems to reflect the increasing influence of neuroscience, together with a growth of interest in evidencebased practice.

In this spirit, we are publishing the abstracts of the research presentations from our Seattle (2010) and Berlin (2011) Congresses. We have research carried out in conventional analytic sessions, in structured interviews, and in laboratory settings; work with patients who have neurological disorders in clinical case reports; and an extensive series of papers using fMRI—all presented by scientists from across the age range and working on every continent.

An additional advantage of publishing these abstracts here is that it allows like-minded individuals to contact each other. We are optimistic that readers interested in any of the dozens of topics will write to those who share common interests and perhaps will initiate a dialogue. Readers from any of the countries represented here who know of neuropsychoanalysis, but not of any local colleagues, can also use the list.

A Reply to Jaak Panksepp

Antonio Damasio

Antonio Damasio

damasio@college.usc.edu

Antonio Damasio  

Let me begin by thanking Oliver Turnbull for inviting me to address Panksepp's review of my book, and Jaak Panksepp for writing a serious review in the first place. Given the admiration I have for his thinking, I regard his review as a privilege. Still, the time I was given to respond to his long text was short and not quite adequate to deal with all the issues it raised. Accordingly, this reply deals only with what I regard as the main issues in the review. Hopefully, brevity will make the important points all the more salient.

It should be clear to readers that Panksepp's thinking and mine are in considerable agreement, on the matter of how the brain generates feelings and sentience at systems/network level (in this reply I do not address the cellular level of the process, nor does he in his review). In a number of passages of his text, however, a reader unacquainted with our work might guess otherwise. This is because Panksepp seems reluctant to agree with my positions except when they are expressed with virtually the same words and nuances that he uses to express his own. For example, there can be no doubt that I believe that nonhuman species—with brains far, far different from ours—are endowed with both feelings and sentience. On p. 26 of Self Comes to Mind, I write:

I am ready to believe that whenever brains begin to generate primordial feelings—and that could be quite early in evolutionary history—organisms acquire an early form of sentience.

Yet Panksepp persists in portraying me as a latecomer to this notion, perhaps even tentative about it. He interprets any word of scientific qualification as hesitation, if not heresy. When I say that all the evidence indicates that animals have feelings and sentience but I add that they have no way of telling it to us, I am not equivocating on my interpretation of the evidence or on my conviction. I am simply alluding to the fact that we must rely on an inference, no matter how well founded the inference is.

Much the same difficulty plagues his comments on the subcortical versus cortical origin of feelings and sentience. There, at least, he can point to the fact that the views I hold today are significantly different from my views of two decades ago. To make a long story short, I began my neuroscience life in the cerebral cortex and in the basal ganglia. While I never neglected the contributions of the hypothalamus and the brainstem to the making of mind, I did not favor them as the beginning of our felt mental life. I believe I was wrong about this. My position changed, and it is still evolving. In some ways, it resembles Panksepp's, although the positions may never become one and the same, for reasons noted below. If they ever do, I will be happy to say so. If not, I hope Panksepp will consider the possible merits of whatever view I will settle on—if ever I settle on one.

Heather Berlin's review is an insightful analysis of the cognitive neuroscience behind unconscious processes at the level of “semantic or inferential processing,” although there are some minor points that are worth re-evaluating. The article seems to conflate the concepts of dissociation put forward by Pierre Janet (the “unconscious compartmentalization of normally integrated mental functions”), the concept of “splitting” (presumably in the Freudian sense), and dissociative disorder as defined by the DSM-IV-TR, despite strong evidence that these are not unitary processes either conceptually and neuropsychologically. Furthermore, the championing of Freud as the figurehead of the dynamic unconscious is perhaps a little misplaced, as the main contribution of Freud was not the concept of unconscious processing, which had a long history before his work and has been well studied since, but the fact that these influences are supposedly interpretable at the level of personal meaning—something that is hard to reconcile with either the majority of evidence from cognitive neuroscience or indeed its conceptual basis. Despite these minor points of contention, the article remains a perceptive and revealing examination of the science of the unconscious.

Ariane Bazan

Ariane Bazan

Brussels, Belgium

ULB CP 122, Avenue Franklin Roosevelt 50, B-1050 Bruxelles (email: Ariane.Bazan@ulb.ac.be).

Ariane Bazan  

efference copy, false connection, phantom, repression, signifier, unconscious

Several clinical case fragments show how a reading of the subject's symptoms at the level of the signifier gives access to its underlying unconscious logic. Freud's “splitting of consciousness” model is proposed to have a neurophysiologic counterpart in LeDoux's model for the processing of emotional stimuli. The language fragments in these dynamics are considered as material phoneme vectors, corresponding to Freud's word-presentation and to Lacan's signifier. Accordingly, neurolinguistic research has uncovered a specific, well-organized lexical brain area in which the words are phonologically encoded. In line with Lacan, psycholinguistic research has shown how the linguistic train always has an ambiguous structure, transiently and unconsciously activating its different meanings, followed by inhibition of the contextually inappropriate meanings. Neurophysiologic research also shows how language is always a motor event. Imminent articulatory intentions that remain without effective execution will therefore give rise to articulatory or phonemic phantoms, searching for relief in substitutive signifiers. A neurophysiologic mechanism for Freudian repression is thus proposed, leading to the return of the repressed in symptoms with a similar phonemic structure though with a radically different meaning. The phonemic phantoms thereby organize the structure of the unconscious by functioning as attractors for the subject's mental energy in its (linguistic) action space.

The Neural Basis of the Dynamic Unconscious

Heather Berlin

Heather Berlin

One Gustave L. Levy Place, Box 1230, New York, NY 10029, U.S.A. (email: heather.berlin@mssm.edu).

Heather Berlin  

unconscious, psychodynamic, repression, suppression, dissociation, neural

A great deal of complex cognitive processing occurs at the unconscious level and affects how humans behave, think, and feel. Scientists are only now beginning to understand how this occurs on the neural level. Understanding the neural basis of consciousness requires an account of the neural mechanisms that underlie both conscious and unconscious thought, and their dynamic interaction. For example, how do conscious impulses, thoughts, or desires become unconscious (e.g., repression) or, conversely, how do unconscious impulses, desires, or motives become conscious (e.g., Freudian slips)? Research taking advantage of advances in technologies, like functional magnetic resonance imaging, has led to a revival and re-conceptualization of some of the key concepts of psychoanalytic theory, but steps toward understanding their neural basis have only just commenced. According to psychoanalytic theory, unconscious dynamic processes defensively remove anxiety-provoking thoughts and impulses from consciousness in response to one's conflicting attitudes. The processes that keep unwanted thoughts from entering consciousness include repression, suppression, and dissociation. In this literature review, studies from psychology and cognitive neuroscience in both healthy and patient populations that are beginning to elucidate the neural basis of these phenomena are discussed and organized within a conceptual framework. Further studies in this emerging field at the intersection of psychoanalytic theory and neuroscience are needed.

Jean Benjamin  

The new approach of our association is centered on the study of interrelationships between psychoanalysis, medicine, and neuroscience. Created in February 2008, the association holds two meetings a year: one “Study Day” and one Symposium where psychoanalysts, neuroscientists, and professors of medical studies participate in scientific exchanges. The SPI members are medical doctors, psychoanalysts, psychotherapists, and neuroscientists. Neuroscience courses are offered by the INSERM laboratory of la Pitié (which includes Lionel Naccache amongst its researchers).

The school of “integrative psychosomatics” considers the human being as a single and global entity called the “psychosomatic unit”; there is not the usual split between body and mind, which has been a dominant influence in Western thought from Anaxagore in the 4th century AD to the present, and has also influenced the different scientific approaches of psychosomatics. The approach is radically different, relying on a new meta-model developed by J. B. Stora in numerous articles published in France. In relation to the neurosciences, we always refer to psycho-neuroendocrinology, psycho-neuroimmunology and neuropsychoanalysis interrelations.

On May 2010, the “Study Day” of the association was centered on the clinical practice of psychosomatics. Papers given included “The Experience and Questions Raised by a Psychoanalyst,” by Marc Dutkiewitcz, vice-chairman of SPI, and “Clinical Experience of a Medical Doctor,” by Dr. Pascale Surugue, oncologist and vice-chair of SPI, with both speakers tackling the psychosomatic clinic with somatic patients. Dr. Myriam Brun-Valicon presented a nephrological case (“Camille”) at the crossroads of medicine and psychoanalysis. Jean Benjamin Stora presented the “heart problems of a famous patient” (Sigmund Freud); this is a psychosomatic approach to Freud's case, with a new study of the medical file by Daniel Thomas, professor of cardiology, and with a new psychoanalytic and psychosomatic elaboration of the clinical material by J. B. Stora. Throughout, the entire program compared the psychosomatic approach to the psychoanalytic approach, embodied by Sandor Ferenczi and Sigmund Freud: the mother role vs. the father role. For example, in psychosomatics, with our patients we adopt a mother role—warm, empathic, and communicative. We don't let our patients remain in silence, which may be very threatening to their health.

The Psychological Clinical Service at Villa Bellombra Rehabilitation Hospital in Bologna supports neurological patients and their caregivers, serving patients suffering from disorders including stroke, multiple sclerosis, dementia, and Parkinson disease. Specific attention is also given to the individual reactions and group dynamics of health workers who take part in the interdisciplinary teams. The service, coordinated by Dr. Marina Farinelli, a clinical psychology specialist and psychoanalytic psychotherapist, integrates clinical rehabilitation practice with psychological and psychotherapeutic interventions based on psychosomatic, psychoanalytic, and neuropsychoanalytic approaches, with the aim of improving diagnosis and therapy throughout the entire rehabilitation process. The Psychological Clinical Service characterizes the hospital and is widely recognized for its innovative approach to rehabilitation; it recently received a request to provide support and collaborate with the local association of stroke patients and caregivers.

The clinical service is also active in research with neurological patients. Some studies are being carried out in collaboration with both Italian and international research institutions, concerning self, emotion, defense mechanisms, attachment, pain, anosognosia, and other topics. For example, the research project “The Impact of Brain Lesion on Internalization/Externalization Processes: A Neuropsychodynamic Study,” began last year in collaboration among Villa Bellombra Rehabilitation Hospital (Dr. Marina Farinelli), the Neuroradiology Unit of the Bellaria Hospital in Bologna (Prof. Marco Leonardi), the Department of Psychology of Bologna University (Prof, Francesca Frassinetti) and the Mind, Brain Imaging and Neuroethics research unit of the Institute of Mental Health Research at the Ottawa University (Prof. Georg Northoff); the project is coordinated by Marina Farinelli and Georg Northoff (supervisor). The project was presented last year during the NPSA Seattle Congress and at meetings held in Bologna and Rome.

Three Emotional Stories: Reflections on Memory, the Imagination, Narrative, and the Self

Siri Hustvedt

Siri Hustvedt

544 2nd Street, Brooklyn, New York, NY 11215, U.S.A. (sirihustvedt55@gmail.com).

Siri Hustvedt   Acclaimed American novelist and essayist.
emotion, imagination, memory, narrative, self, time

In this essay, I propose that memory and the imagination partake of the same mental processes: that they are driven by emotion and often take narrative form. Through reflective self-consciousness, human beings are not bound to the phenomenal present. They can recall themselves in the past, imagine themselves in the future, and inhabit fictive realms. Borrowing William James's distinction between narrative thought and reasoning, as well as the difference between first- and third-person perspectives, I describe the varying approaches of fiction, psychoanalysis, and neuroscience to remembering and imagining. Conscious episodic memories are consolidated by emotion, but they are also reconsolidated—subject to Freud's “deferred action”—to fictionalizing over time. Story organizes the affective material of memory into a temporal, linguistic schema that is necessarily dialogical: “I” implies “you.” As articulated representation, narrative recollection inevitably distances and cools past emotion. This is not true of involuntary and traumatic memories that are sensorimotor, affective replays of an event, are not codified in language, and cannot be located in a subjective time or space. Research into self- versus other-“processing” in the brain has largely failed to understand that at an explicit, representational level, there is no difference between memories and fantasies about self and other. Culling insights from Freud and research in neuroscience and phenomenology, I argue that a core bodily, affective, timeless self is the ground of the narrative, temporal self, of autobiographical memory, and of fiction and that the secret to creativity lies not in the so-called higher cognitive processes, but in dreamlike reconfigurations of emotional meanings that take place unconsciously.

“You are a Cannibal”—A Case Report: Psychoanalysis of an Adolescent Boy with Bifrontal Lesions (Part 1: The First Year)

Zsofia Kovacs , Daphne Stock and Günther Bernert

Günther Bernert

Gottfried von Preyer'sches Kinderspital, Schrankenberggasse 31, 1100 Vienna, Austria (zsofia.kovacs@wienkav.at).

Günther Bernert  

clinical neuropsychoanalysis, frontal lobe pathology, dysexecutive syndrome, child analysis, adolescence, traumatic brain injury

Accompanying a male adolescent out of the darkness of being unable to differentiate between inside and outside, between being a boy or a girl—the psychoanalytic journey is described from both a clinical and a theoretical perspective. Based on Sigmund Freud's metapsychology, psychoanalytic concepts such as regression, defense mechanisms of the ego such as projection and introjection, and features of the primary process are illuminated. Special emphasis is placed on changes in body schema and the role of language in reality testing. The therapeutic process cannot be understood without reference to the psychoanalytic concept of the ego and its early development. Using neuroimaging evidence, results of neuropsychological assessment, and excerpts of the ongoing therapy sessions, the pieces of the boy's history are put together alongside the reconstruction-surgery of the frontal cranial bones.

Jaak Panksepp

Jaak Panksepp

jpanksepp@vetmed.wsu.edu

Jaak Panksepp  

A personal perspective on Antonio Damasio's vision of brain/mind evolution in Self Comes to Mind. Is there only one type of consciousness? And was William James right about the origins of emotional feelings?

We all know that the gap between neuronal function and subjective experience remains unbridged. In the current generation, Antonio Damasio has been among the more vigorous pioneers to begin constructing the requisite bridges. In his most recent effort, Self Comes to Mind (henceforth SCM), Damasio once again recruits his deep knowledge and imagination to move forward this critically important neuroscientific project.

For general readers, this is a terrific book—an intriguing journey through the human mind, the self, and consciousness. For those immersed in either thinking or working on these issues, there are bound to be many bones of contention. That should be no surprise. It is standard practice in science, especially when confusion and controversy stubbornly prevail in areas that abound with fascinating but empirically unresolved issues. In the arena of consciousness studies, there are currently abundant verbal solutions, and abundant neural correlates, but rather little causal neuroscientific data. My goal here will be to give an overview of SCM and then gnaw a bit on some of the remaining contentions. I regret how long this review has turned out to be, but that is largely due to the fact that it turned out to be very difficult to review this remarkable book, partly because Damasio was explicitly moving toward my own long-held position, but often in ways that seemed, in my estimation, more compelling than they actually were.

In SCM, rich with abstractions, Damasio develops a refurbished version of the bottom-up vision of mind that he initiated with The Feeling of What Happens (1999). Consciousness is grounded on a proto-self that provides a primordial infrastructure for higher self-concepts that help create conscious awareness along with a background of textured autobiographical memories. Wisely, Damasio constructs his foundational proto-self from the most primal ancestral brain mechanisms that regulate our basic life needs (bodily homeostasis). To this extent, Damasio's new vision of the evolution of “the self” certainly has abundant implications for understanding consciousness and perhaps the affective life. I personally found the attempt to ground consciousness to sensory functions rather off the mark at the foundational level, for all too easily that tends to leave the organism itself, with all of its wonderful action tendencies, too far out of the picture.

Embodied Simulation, Mirror Neurons, and the Reenactment of Trauma in Early Childhood

Theodore Gaensbauer

Theodore Gaensbauer

3400 East Bayaud Avenue, Suite 460, Denver, CO 80209, U.S.A. (email: Tgaensbauer@aol.com).

Theodore Gaensbauer  

early childhood, early memory, embodied simulation, mirror neurons, trauma, reenactment

The question of why children would repeatedly replicate painful, frightening events in their behavior or play, often in very destructive ways, has long challenged clinicians and researchers alike. The recent identification of “mirror neurons” in the premotor cortex of macaque monkeys and the ongoing elucidation of their role in facilitating empathic resonance with, and imitation of, the observed actions of others in both monkeys and humans have opened up new perspectives on this question. Initially, an overview of post-traumatic reenactment behaviors as they are manifested in young children is presented, highlighting important developmental and therapeutic issues that such behavior raises. Next, recent research on embodiment, early imitation, and mirror neuron functioning is reviewed, with an emphasis on those aspects most relevant to the clinical manifestations of early trauma. The significance of this recent research for furthering our understanding of the mechanisms underlying posttraumatic reenactment is outlined. In addition, some of the implications of this research for our understanding of the nature of early traumatic memories, the availability of such memories for conscious processing, and the role of such memories in the reenactment of preverbal trauma are described. Finally, the clinical implications of this work for the fashioning of effective therapeutic interventions is discussed.

The “Dynamic Unconscious” may Be Experienced: Can We Discuss Unconscious Emotions when there are no Adequate Measures of Affective Change?

Jaak Panksepp

Jaak Panksepp

Pullman, WA, U.S.A.

Jaak Panksepp  

affective consciousness, phenomenal consciousness, emotional experiences, dynamic unconscious, intentionality, signal detection

The brain has many deeply unconscious neural processes, but the realm of phenomenal consciousness (qualia) rather than “awareness” is the critical issue whether there is nothing relevant in mind while so-called “dynamically unconscious” processes are operating in the brain. Concepts such as “conscious awareness” are one step above phenomenal experiences and can easily lead to confusions about what is or is not experienced during dynamically “unconscious” emotional information processing. If one does not explicitly evaluate for the presence of affective phenomenal experiential shifts, with the most sensitive and relevant measures, one can fall into the trap of calling something unconscious when it is simply not being processed in higher order “awareness.” I provide examples of where the failure to monitor affective experiential shifts has too easily led investigators to place experienced aspects of mind into the unconscious, based more on their limited methodologies rather than on the absence of experiential affective shifts that pass through the mind experimentally unnoticed. Such lapses in experimental control may have had invidious, but currently unevaluated, effects on the very substantial review of available research and thinking on the “dynamic unconscious” that Heather Berlin superbly summarizes.

Editors' Introduction

Oliver Turnbull and David Olds

David Olds

David Olds  

Target Article

Our Target Article in this issue, “The Neural Basis of the Dynamic Unconscious,” is a trove of information integrating psychoanalytic and neuroscientific information. The author, Heather Berlin, surveys the extensive research showing that subliminal (and thereby subconscious) stimuli have complex effects in the brain and also on later behavior and conscious thought. Stimuli that are too briefly presented, or are “masked” by a subsequent—usually conscious—stimulus, will not reach awareness. But there are other mental processes that make use of subliminal processing of high-level brain functioning. Most dramatic are those that occur in the presence of brain lesions that produce modifications in conscious awareness. Well-known examples are blindsight, hemineglect, procedural learning in amnesia, and split-brain syndromes with corpus callosum lesions. In these cases, where conscious awareness of the stimulus is not possible, there are influences on behavior that show considerable below-consciousness processing. For instance, a blindsighted person, unaware of seeing anything, may still avoid running into objects in his or her path.

Early research on the conscious/unconscious interface dealt mostly with these phenomena involving cognitive processes, with little interest in the influence of the emotional and motivational aspects of mind. However, it has become increasingly evident that various rather “intellectual” processes, such as choices and decisions, are influenced by unconscious motivations and by the need to avoid emotionally aversive consequences.

The article presents much of the research that has examined the defenses that appear to maintain the boundaries of such unconscious aspects of mental life. Analytically oriented readers will be all too aware that these defenses appear to have evolved to help a person avoid the discomfort associated with unhappy truths, and their associated painful affects. In this review article, we are presented with current research into three major defense mechanisms: repression, suppression, and dissociation.

Georgina Torbet  

“The Truth about Lying”

“So you did, you know,” the Red Queen said to Alice. “Always speak the truth—think before you speak—and write it down afterwards.”

“I'm sure I didn't mean—” Alice was beginning, but the Red Queen interrupted her impatiently.

“That's just what I complain of! You should have meant!”

Karim, A. A., Schneider, M., Lotze, M., Veit, R., Sauseng, P., Braun, C., & Birbaumer, N. (2010). The truth about lying: Inhibition of the anterior prefrontal cortex improves deceptive behavior.Cerebral Cortex, 20 (1): 205-213.

Neuroethics is a field very much in vogue, with many experimenters clamoring to provide neuroscientific explanations for moral behaviors. Too often, this enthusiasm translates to poor experimental methodology and broadly unsupported causal assertions. Karim et al., however, have used robust methods to provided intriguing primary evidence for a causal role of the anterior prefrontal cortex (aPFC) in deceptive behavior. The area is certainly ripe for further study.

The authors used transcranial direct-current stimulation (tDCS)—a technique that disables particular areas of the brain by stimulating them with an electrical current—to investigate lying and deceptive behavior. By stimulating the aPFC, they were able to induce a small but significant improvement in deceptive behavior. While aPFC has previously been indicated to be involved in ethical decision-making, this study provides new evidence of its causal role in moral behaviors.

Their methodology is commendably ecologically valid: They asked participants to steal a wallet left in another room and then answer questions posed by an interrogator. Mimicking a police interview, the participant had to choose which questions to answer truthfully and which to answer with a lie. A “lying quotient” (LQ) was calculated using the ratio of lies to incriminating questions to truthful answers to nonincriminating questions. An effective deception would be one that not only did not provide compromising information, but also gave truthful answers to questions that an innocent subject could answer. Participants were motivated by an agreement that they could keep the money in the wallet if they succeeded in deceiving the interrogator.

Reflection and Representation

“Do you ever wonder if the guy in the puddle is real, and you're just a reflection of him?”

Calvin & Hobbes

What relation exists between objects in the world and the way that these objects are modeled by our minds? The representational theory of mind proposes that our experience of objects within the world is mediated through mental representations—that is, mental symbols that stand for each object or idea. The idea of mental representations is explored in this digest through research in psychology, neuroscience, and psychoanalysis. The internal representation of our bodies and how this constructs subjective experience is examined by David et al. on the feeling of agency and Pyka et al. on the neural basis for hypnotic paralysis; while how the actions of others are represented in our brain is covered by Glenberg et al. on mirror neurons. The representational qualities of our memories and how this may be affected by modern technology is examined by Sparrow et al. on the “Google effect”; and the interaction between cultural representations and individual behavior is investigated in terms of gender by Alanko et al. on gender-atypical behavior and in terms of social ills and mental disorder by Morgan on reification and schizophrenia.

David, N., Stenzel, A., Schneider, T. R., & Engel, A. K. (2011). The feeling of agency: Empirical indicators for a pre-reflective level of action awareness.Frontiers in Psychology, 2 (149): 1-8.

The concept of the feeling of agency is of interest given its status as an object of research in cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and phenomenology. The sense of being an agent of an action is so inherent to human experience that it is difficult to imagine its loss or destructuring. Excepting simple reflexive actions, such as your leg jerking when a tendon is struck on the knee, our feeling of agency is deep-rooted and inherent. It is thus hard to comprehend the experiences reported by some people with psychosis of feeling as though they were not the agents of their complex movements, actions, or speech, as in the case of a psychotic patient who may claim that someone else is causing his arm to move. In the philosophical terminology, feeling of agency is “prereflective”—that is, first-personal on a fundamental level, before reflection and conscious processing.

Embodied Simulation Theory: Imagination and Narrative

Vittorio Gallese

Vittorio Gallese

Italy

Vittorio Gallese  

aesthetic experience, embodied narratology, embodied simulation, imagination, mirror neurons

The timely and thought-provoking essay by Siri Hustvedt provides a fascinating account of the relationship between imagination and memory and discusses this relationship against the background of different disciplines like psychoanalysis, cognitive neuroscience, and phenomenology. Hustvedt sheds new light from the inside on the process of artistic creativity by emphasizing that the bodily affective self is at the roots of the narrative self. In the present commentary, I present and briefly discuss recent scientific results corroborating Hustvedt's thesis and propose how embodied simulation theory can account for many aspects of the relationship between artistic production and its aesthetic experience.

Mark Solms and Oliver Turnbull

Oliver Turnbull

South Africa

U.K.

Gwynedd LL57 2AS, U.K. (email: o.turnbull@bangor.ac.uk).

Oliver Turnbull  

neuropsychoanalysis, history of science, Freud, mind-body problem, dual-aspect monism

This article briefly surveys the interdisciplinary field of neuroscience and psychoanalysis (“neuropsychoanalysis”) and also addresses some of the criticisms that the field has encountered. First, the article reviews the historical foundations of neuropsychoanalysis, including both theoretical and technical questions of whether an interdiscipline is appropriate. Second, it discusses the philosophical foundations of the field, including the position of dual-aspect monism. Third, the article examines the scientific foundations, with a discussion of whether analytic work with neurological patients represents an optimal point of contact between the disciplines. Finally, the article engages with the issue of what neuropsychoanalysis is not, covering issues such as “speculation versus empirical research,” and the question of whether neuropsychoanalysis represents a new “school” of psychoanalysis.

In 2010, several activities were carried out by members of the Vienna Neuro-Psychoanalysis Study Group.

In spring 2010, a national joint meeting was held at the Vienna Psychoanalytic Academy by members of the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society, the Vienna Psychoanalytic Association, and the Institute of Computer Technology, Technical University Vienna. The workshop focused on Freud's structural model of the mental apparatus and its application in computer technology, representing a follow-up meeting of an international symposium held in 2007 in Vienna (ENF 2007, “Emulating the Mind”), then coorganized by the Technical University Vienna (Institute of Computer Technology) and the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society. The organizers of the workshop mentioned above also applied for funding of an international so-called exploratory workshop by the European Science Foundation, to be held in 2011.

Earlier this year, a member of the study group, Gerald Wiest, attended the Research Training Program of the International Psychoanalytical Association at Yale University, organized by Linda Mayes and Peter Fonagy, and presented a prospective research project on the assessment of affective states in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy. Another IPA-supported study, entitled “Emotional Experience during Transient Hemispheric Inactivation: Neuropsychoanalytic Investigations using the Wada-Test,” is still ongoing. The study investigates unilateral processing of affects in patients undergoing presurgical evaluation for epilepsy surgery.

Two neuropsychoanalytic papers have been published by members of the Viennese Study Group in 2010. The first paper, published in Psyche, deals with the empirical dimension of primary-process mentation (Wiest, 2010). The second paper, published in Neuropsychoanalysis, reports on the neuropsychoanalytic findings in a patient with bilateral lesions of the amygdala (Wiest & Brainin, 2010). In addition, Gerald Wiest published a neuropsychoanalytic book in late 2009, entitled Hierarchies in Brain, Mind, and Behavior (with a foreword by Mark Solms).

The Cognitive Unconscious Seems Related to the Dynamic Unconscious—But it's not the Whole Story

Maggie Zellner

Maggie Zellner

New York, U.S.A.

Maggie Zellner  

unconscious, external stimuli, endogenous processes, object representations

Psychoanalytically minded thinkers can feel optimistic that our belief in a dynamic unconscious—motivational, emotional, and cognitive processes that happen outside of awareness, yet influence our conscious experience and behavior—is finding increasing support in cognitive psychology and the neurosciences. Heather Berlin ably summarizes a wealth of findings indicating that our feelings and actions are influenced by stimuli that are not perceived or attended to. Because these findings emerge from experimental work, in which conditions are controlled by the investigator, skeptics outside of psychodynamically friendly circles are now more likely to accept that unconscious processes must be taken into account. This is surely good for our field. However, because the nature of experimental work relies on external stimuli, presented under control of an investigator, we still have a long way to go toward understanding the neural nature of those aspects of the dynamic unconscious that arise from within the subject, including endogenous drive processes and an internal world of mental representations.

The Anna Karenina Theory of the Unconscious

Ned Block

Ned Block

New York, U.S.A.

Ned Block  

Anna Karenina; unconscious; phenomenal consciousness; access consciousness; dream; anosognosia

The Anna Karenina theory says: all conscious states are alike; each unconscious state is unconscious in its own way. This paper argues that many components have to function properly to produce consciousness, but failure in any one of many different ones can yield an unconscious state in different ways. In that sense the Anna Karenina theory is true. But in another respect it is false: kinds of unconsciousness depend on kinds of consciousness.

Christian Salas  

In the history of neuropsychological rehabilitation there have been books that promote a change of paradigm. These books possess a peculiar transitional quality. They are rooted in old theories and concepts, but at the same time they try to break free from them, in an attempt to build up something new. Rather than systematizing what we already know, they point in novel directions, providing possibilities and inspiration. This book is one of those books.

I will try to justify such statements. But in order to do so, I will have to put this book in the context of how the field of neuropsychological rehabilitation has evolved. Much of the early work with people who suffered a brain injury was devoted to the comprehension of the “disordered mind” (Prigatano, 1991) and the mechanisms by which these altered cognitive functions could be restored (Goldstein, 1942; Luria, 1973). Although this first era offered a priceless understanding on the relationship between brain and psychological processes, it was not until the 1990s, with Principles of Neuropsychological Rehabilitation (Prigatano, 1999), that the “wounded soul” (Prigatano, 1991) of brain-injured patients was systematically introduced as a focus of rehabilitation. This new emphasis on the patient's experience of the injury, and on the mechanisms by which personality and injury dynamically interact, was a groundbreaking proposition.

In the same year, another book redefined one of the most emblematic components of the field, cognitive rehabilitation. In Case Studies in Neuropsychological Rehabilitation, Barbara Wilson (1999) offered a detailed description of patients with diverse neuropsychological impairments, and the strategies used to help them restore and compensate their deficits. The most powerful message of this book was that cognitive rehabilitation was, in essence, a means for returning to emotionally meaningful activities. Thus, the main goal of cognitive rehabilitation was not to restore a previous level of cognitive functioning, especially considering that many patients never accomplish it, but returning to satisfying levels of social participation by recovering those important roles that define us.
